questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This figure shows six electrodes positioned across the chest wall and lateral thorax for an ECG. The electrical activity recorded by these six leads represents the heart in which anatomical plane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The horizontal (transverse) plane

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mid-clavicular plane

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sagittal plane

choices.label: D
choices.text: The frontal (coronal) plane

choices.label: E
choices.text: The oblique long-axis plane

explanation.summary: The precordial (chest) leads V1 through V6 encircle the thorax and view the heart's depolarization in the horizontal plane, complementing the limb leads that view the frontal plane. Together they localize activity in two perpendicular planes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The precordial (chest) leads V1 through V6 encircle the thorax and view the heart's depolarization in the horizontal plane, complementing the limb leads that view the frontal plane. Together they localize activity in two perpendicular planes.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: The Einthoven triangle on the left records a strongly positive complex, and the heart schematic on the right shows the corresponding spread of depolarization. Why is this lead (from right arm to left leg) normally strongly upright?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This lead measures only the SA node discharge

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wave of depolarization spreads toward the left leg (positive electrode), roughly parallel to this lead's axis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The wave travels perpendicular to this lead's axis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The left leg electrode records atrial repolarization directly

choices.label: E
choices.text: The positive electrode lies over the right atrium

explanation.summary: In lead II the positive electrode is at the left leg; ventricular depolarization spreads from the AV node down and to the left, nearly parallel to and toward this electrode, producing a tall upright QRS.
explanation.whyCorrect: In lead II the positive electrode is at the left leg; ventricular depolarization spreads from the AV node down and to the left, nearly parallel to and toward this electrode, producing a tall upright QRS.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This recording displays the standard 12 tracings plus a continuous strip along the bottom. What is the purpose of that additional bottom tracing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A stress-test comparison tracing

choices.label: B
choices.text: A rhythm strip providing a continuous single-lead recording to assess rhythm over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: A calibration reference pulse for amplitude

choices.label: D
choices.text: A recording of the precordial leads only

choices.label: E
choices.text: A separate tracing of atrial activity alone

explanation.summary: A standard 12-lead ECG records brief segments of each lead; the long bottom strip is a continuous rhythm strip (often lead II or V1) used to evaluate rate and rhythm across many beats.
explanation.whyCorrect: A standard 12-lead ECG records brief segments of each lead; the long bottom strip is a continuous rhythm strip (often lead II or V1) used to evaluate rate and rhythm across many beats.

questions.stem: This 12-lead layout is color-coded to group leads by the region of myocardium they best represent. Leads II, III, and aVF together primarily view which cardiac wall?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Septal wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lateral wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inferior wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Posterior wall

explanation.summary: Leads II, III, and aVF are the inferior leads; grouping leads by territory (inferior, lateral, anterior, septal) helps localize ischemia or infarction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leads II, III, and aVF are the inferior leads; grouping leads by territory (inferior, lateral, anterior, septal) helps localize ischemia or infarction.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This panel shows the six frontal-plane limb leads, each with its electrode polarity, axis direction, and resulting complex. What do these six leads together allow the clinician to determine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean electrical axis of the heart in the frontal plane

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ejection fraction of the left ventricle

choices.label: C
choices.text: The absolute serum potassium concentration

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coronary artery anatomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: The oxygen saturation of arterial blood

explanation.summary: The six limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) view the heart from different angles in the frontal plane; comparing their deflections lets one calculate the mean QRS electrical axis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The six limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) view the heart from different angles in the frontal plane; comparing their deflections lets one calculate the mean QRS electrical axis.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This diagram overlays the directional vectors of the limb and precordial leads on the torso. What key concept about ECG leads does it illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Precordial leads measure only atrial activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lead placement does not affect the recorded signal

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vectors represent coronary blood flow direction

choices.label: D
choices.text: All leads record identical waveforms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each lead views the heart's electrical activity from a different angle/orientation

explanation.summary: The multiple arrows show that each lead has its own axis, so the same depolarization is seen from many directions; combining these views gives a three-dimensional picture of cardiac electrical activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The multiple arrows show that each lead has its own axis, so the same depolarization is seen from many directions; combining these views gives a three-dimensional picture of cardiac electrical activity.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This torso schematic contrasts two recording planes of the ECG. The limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) record activity in which of these planes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The horizontal (transverse) plane

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sagittal plane

choices.label: C
choices.text: The oblique plane

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coronal blood-flow plane

choices.label: E
choices.text: The frontal plane

explanation.summary: The limb leads view the heart in the frontal plane, whereas the precordial (chest) leads view it in the horizontal plane; together they give orthogonal perspectives.
explanation.whyCorrect: The limb leads view the heart in the frontal plane, whereas the precordial (chest) leads view it in the horizontal plane; together they give orthogonal perspectives.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This diagram shows the placement of the four color-coded limb electrodes for a standard ECG. What is the primary function of the electrode positioned on the right leg?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It measures right atrial depolarization directly

choices.label: B
choices.text: It serves as the neutral ground/reference electrode

choices.label: C
choices.text: It records the precordial V1 signal

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the positive electrode for lead II

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the exploring electrode for aVR

explanation.summary: The right leg (green) electrode is a ground/reference used for noise reduction and does not contribute directly to the recorded limb-lead vectors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The right leg (green) electrode is a ground/reference used for noise reduction and does not contribute directly to the recorded limb-lead vectors.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This figure shows how a single wave of cardiac depolarization produces different ECG deflections at the top and a normal upright complex at right. What determines whether the recorded deflection is upward or downward?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The direction of the depolarization wave relative to the positive electrode (toward = upward, away = downward)

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absolute magnitude of the resting membrane potential

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heart rate at the moment of recording

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distance between the SA and AV nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: The total mass of ventricular myocardium

explanation.summary: An ECG deflection is positive when the depolarization wave travels toward the positive (recording) electrode and negative when it travels away, so orientation of the wave, not its size alone, sets the polarity.
explanation.whyCorrect: An ECG deflection is positive when the depolarization wave travels toward the positive (recording) electrode and negative when it travels away, so orientation of the wave, not its size alone, sets the polarity.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: On this normal ECG tracing, which electrical event does the tall central deflection (R, flanked by Q and S) represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ventricular depolarization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atrial repolarization

choices.label: C
choices.text: SA node automaticity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ventricular repolarization

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atrial depolarization

explanation.summary: The QRS complex reflects rapid depolarization of the ventricular myocardium; the P wave is atrial depolarization and the T wave is ventricular repolarization.
explanation.whyCorrect: The QRS complex reflects rapid depolarization of the ventricular myocardium; the P wave is atrial depolarization and the T wave is ventricular repolarization.

questions.imageRef: repic-729_Brick Exchange - Electrocardiogram_ Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)_p15_1.png

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: This figure aligns the ECG waves with atrial and ventricular action potentials and tension curves. Why is atrial repolarization not seen as a distinct wave on the ECG?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atria do not repolarize during the cardiac cycle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It occurs during the T wave and cancels it

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is buried within the large QRS complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: It happens before the P wave and is filtered out

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is recorded only in the precordial leads

explanation.summary: Atrial repolarization is low in amplitude and coincides in time with ventricular depolarization, so it is masked by (buried in) the much larger QRS complex.
explanation.whyCorrect: Atrial repolarization is low in amplitude and coincides in time with ventricular depolarization, so it is masked by (buried in) the much larger QRS complex.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: The left trace (labeled phases 0-4) is aligned with the ECG on the right. What does phase 2, the sustained plateau, of this cardiac ventricular action potential represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium influx balancing potassium efflux, prolonging depolarization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Potassium efflux driving rapid repolarization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Funny-current (If) driven spontaneous depolarization

choices.label: D
choices.text: The resting membrane potential maintained by the Na/K pump

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid sodium influx causing the upstroke

explanation.summary: Phase 2 is the plateau of the ventricular action potential, produced by inward Ca2+ current balancing outward K+ current; this prolonged depolarization underlies the refractory period and corresponds to the ST segment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase 2 is the plateau of the ventricular action potential, produced by inward Ca2+ current balancing outward K+ current; this prolonged depolarization underlies the refractory period and corresponds to the ST segment.

questions.topicName: Electrocardiogram: Fundamentals and Lead Placement (1 of 2)
questions.stem: The top graph plots transmembrane potentials of two adjacent normal cells (VA earlier, VB later) and the bottom graph shows the resulting extracellular tracing. Why does a biphasic (upward then downward) signal appear in the extracellular recording?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both cells depolarize simultaneously, canceling all signal

choices.label: B
choices.text: The signal reflects the resting potential of a single cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: A voltage difference exists between the two cells during depolarization and again during repolarization, generating current flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only repolarization produces any extracellular deflection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ion channels remain closed throughout the cycle

explanation.summary: An extracellular electrode senses potential differences between regions; as depolarization and then repolarization sweep across the two cells at different times, transient voltage gradients drive current and produce the biphasic deflection, the basis of the ECG.
explanation.whyCorrect: An extracellular electrode senses potential differences between regions; as depolarization and then repolarization sweep across the two cells at different times, transient voltage gradients drive current and produce the biphasic deflection, the basis of the ECG.
